positive.outline-conclusion:
## Setup

Install the package with npm, then copy the sample token into a local env file. Most teams keep that file out of version control. If you already run a proxy, point the base URL at it before the first call. A wrong port here shows up later as a timeout, which wastes an afternoon. Windows users should set the cache directory by hand.

## Usage

Call run() with a path. It returns a promise that resolves to a report object; the report carries counts, offsets, and any warnings the reader produced. Streaming mode exists for very large inputs, though most callers never need it. Prefer the sync helper when your input fits in memory, because backpressure handling adds real complexity for no gain. The CLI wraps the same entry point.

## Troubleshooting

Read the log first. Almost every failure prints a stack trace with the offending line number, and the trace names the rule that rejected the input. Turn on verbose output when the trace looks empty. Corrupted caches cause the strangest reports, so clearing the cache directory is worth trying early. Network errors retry three times before they surface, which can make a fast failure look slow.

## Limits

Two gigabytes is the practical ceiling for a single document. Beyond that, split the input by chapter and merge the reports afterwards. Nested archives are skipped rather than expanded, and symlinks outside the project root raise an error instead of following quietly. Nothing here is configurable yet, though a flag is planned for the next minor release.

## Reporting a bug

Open an issue with the failing input attached, or a reduced case if the file is private. Version numbers matter more than stack traces here, since the parser changed shape twice last year. Maintainers usually reply within two working days.

## Conclusion

As we've seen, setup takes one command, usage is a single function call, and troubleshooting just means reading the log file.
